audits.claim: Sentence-final speech levels: 'seven classical, four to six alive'.
audits.source_locator: Korean speech levels (English Wikipedia, retrieved full text), lead paragraph and per-level 'Currency' rows: Hasoseo-che (uncommon), Hasipsio-che / Haeyo-che / Haera-che / Hae-che (common), Hao-che and Hage-che (less common)
audits.source_excerpt: There are seven verb paradigms or speech levels in Korean, and each level has its own unique set of verb endings … Hasoseo-che is now used mainly in movies or dramas set in the Joseon era and in religious speech.
audits.retrieval_method: FetchURL full-page text retrieval (native tool); corroborating full texts: Song-Bradford (1979) PhD dissertation PDF downloaded via https://ndownloader.figshare.com/files/41884662 (Aura/American University record https://aura.american.edu/articles/thesis/REFLECTIONS_OF_STATUS_AND_INTIMACY_IN_KOREAN_SPEECH_LEVELS_ENGLISH_CODE_AND_THEIR_USE_IN_DYADIC_CONVERSATIONS_BETWEEN_BILINGUAL_KOREANS/23887002/1) and pdftotext; Ku (2014) ANU sub-thesis already retrieved in the prior ledger row; institutional host korean.go.kr retested with curl and timed out again (exit 28); encykorea.aks.ac.kr reachable (HTTP 200) but its keyword search endpoint redirects to a 404 shell from this environment, so no AKS article text was retrievable
audits.basis: The two halves of the count are now each attached to retrieved text, under tradition-specific scopes rather than one universal count. (a) 'Seven classical': the retrieved full text presents the traditional seven-style scheme (합쇼체, 하소서체, 하오체, 하게체, 해라체, 해요체, 해체), with the archaic very-formal-polite style (하소서체) confined to period drama and religious language — resolving the prior round's specific blocker that no retrieved source attributed the seven count. (b) 'Four to six alive': the scholarly tradition counts six modern styles with divergent groupings — Song-Bradford (1979: ~150–152), retrieved in full, surveys Martin (1964, 1969), Yang (1972) and Hwang (1975): 'Hwang prefers to divide the six styles into four levels so that four of the levels are defined as "formal" alternants, while two of the styles, -yo and -0, are "informal" alternants', and notes 'Although all linguists do not treat them in the same way, most, including Martin and Hwang, see a categorical difference between other levels and the -yo and -0 (panmal) levels'; the prior-round retrieval of Ku (2014) gives six levels of which four are commonly in use. Per-level currency in the retrieved seven-style presentation (four common, two less common, one archaic) makes 'four to six alive' read exactly as four common levels up to six when the two marginal ones (하오체, 하게체) are counted as alive, with the archaic seventh excluded. Both numbers of the entry's claim are therefore supported as tradition-scoped statements, not as one universal count.
audits.coupling_implication: For the entry's language × social-structure coupling: the level inventory is classification-relative (seven-style classical scheme vs six-style modern scholarly schemes vs four-level groupings inside those six), so a fictional world should fix who counts the levels (academy, etiquette manuals) and which archaic levels survive in which liturgical or courtly domains — alive-count tracks institution, not a timeless grammar fact.
audits.limits: The seven-style enumeration is a tertiary encyclopedia page, not a primary grammar; its citations include the entry's registered source (Lee & Ramsey 2000) and Korean grammar references, but Lee & Ramsey (2000) itself was again not retrieved. The National Institute of Korean Language's own count remains unverified: korean.go.kr timed out (curl exit 28) on 2026-10-17, as in the prior attempt; the Academy of Korean Studies encyclopedia is reachable but its keyword search route is not usable headlessly (302 to 404), so no AKS article content was retrieved. OCR of the 1979 microfilm scan shows artifacts (e.g. '-0' for '-∅'); normalized without change of sense. Verdict scope: the count claim as tradition-scoped inventory and usage range; not an assertion that any single institution fixes seven (or six) as canonical.

audits.source_locator: Haviland, John B., 'Guugu Yimithirr Brother-in-Law Language' (chapter version; a version first appeared in Language in Society 8: 365–393), footnote 3 quoting Dixon (1971: 437–8); supported by the retrieved full text of English Wikipedia 'Avoidance speech', Dyirbal examples citing Dixon 1980, Section 3.3 'Speech and song styles: Avoidance styles', pp. 58–65 (jijan example at pp. 61–64)
audits.source_excerpt: Dyalnguy contains far fewer words than Guwal — something on the order of a quarter as many. … it still being possible to say in Dyalnguy everything that can be said in Guwal.
audits.retrieval_method: PDF downloaded from the already-registered URL with curl and converted with pdftotext; the Dixon sentence is retrieved verbatim inside Haviland's footnote 3 quotation with page cite 1971: 437–8; Wikipedia 'Avoidance speech' retrieved as full-page text with FetchURL; primary-text routes that failed: archive.org scans of Dixon 1972 (dyirballanguageo00dixo), Dixon 1980 (languagesofaustr0000dixo), Sohn 1999, the Semantics reader (Dixon 1971) and Dixon's 1983 memoir are all lending-restricted (inside.php returns 403 'Item not available'), and OpenAlex lists the specialist chapters (Dixon 2015 OUP 'Jalnguy, the mother-in-law speech style in Dyirbal'; 2025 DeGruyter festschrift chapters) as closed with no OA location; ANU repository bitstream endpoints returned 401
audits.basis: The prior round left this unresolved because Dixon's own formulation was unretrieved. It is now retrieved, via Haviland's verbatim quotation of Dixon (1971: 437–8): jalnguy has on the order of a quarter as many words as guwal, exploits every syntactic and semantic device to keep its vocabulary minimal, and yet 'it still being possible to say in Dyalnguy everything that can be said in Guwal'. This supports the entry's phrase in the functional sense the bullet intends (speakers switch wholly to a distinct vocabulary with full expressive coverage; the presence-triggered switch itself was separately supported in SR-REG-06) while the same retrieved texts exclude the erroneous one-to-one reading: the correspondences are 'often rather complex' and one-to-many (Haviland, quoting Dixon and describing the parallel Guugu Yimidhirr BIL lexicon as 'usually one-to-many'; retrieved Wikipedia text citing Dixon 1980 pp. 61–64 gives the Dyirbal example of one word, jijan, covering all lizards that guwal differentiates). So: complete replacement in expressive function — supported; per-lexeme synonymy — contradicted by the same retrieved evidence and expressly not part of the verdict.
audits.coupling_implication: Language × kinship-taboo coupling confirmed at the lexical-economy level: an avoidance register is a collapsed-lexicon design (roughly a quarter of the everyday vocabulary plus circumlocution), not a synonym table — the strongest design guidance for a fictional world is to build few high-frequency avoidance stems and rules for deriving the rest, and to expect reduced lexical differentiation inside taboo talk.
audits.limits: Dixon's primary texts (1971, 1972, 1980) remain unretrieved: all archive.org scans are lending-restricted and the OUP/DeGruyter/CUP chapters are closed access, so the Dixon sentence is verified only through Haviland's quoted translation of it (with his page citation), not from the 1971 page itself. The retrieved Wikipedia article is tertiary, citing Dixon 1980 §3.3 pp. 58–65. Haviland's target language is Guugu Yimidhirr; his cases of everyday words with 'no BIL equivalent whatsoever' (his Fig. 4, type D) are Guugu Yimidhirr facts and are not projected onto Dyirbal, for which the retrieved Dixon quotation instead asserts full sayability with a quarter-size lexicon. The verdict preserves the entry's claim scope: no marker was renamed or cleared and no corpus text was edited.
